target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday will remove scheduling barriers and help low-income voters
objection: A federal holiday does not by itself guarantee paid time off for private-sector workers, especially in retail, food service, and other hourly jobs. Because those workers may still have to work or lose pay, the holiday could leave low-income workers no better off than before and may benefit higher-income workers more.

target: AG1’s reliance on a national holiday as the main solution to voting barriers
objection: More direct policies—such as laws requiring employers to provide time to vote with pay protections, plus automatic or opt-out voter registration—are more reliable ways to increase turnout and reduce missed voting opportunities than simply declaring Election Day a holiday.

target: AG1’s assertion that a holiday reduces scheduling conflict for the workers who need help most
objection: The workers with the hardest time voting are often low-income hourly employees in sectors like retail, food service, and caregiving, which frequently keep operating even on holidays. So changing the calendar does not reliably change the schedules that block their voting.

target: AG1’s view that holiday status directly solves wage and time problems for hourly workers
objection: A national holiday changes the date but does not itself create paid leave or stop private employers from keeping staff on duty. Therefore, workers may still have to choose between working, losing pay, or using scarce PTO to vote.

target: AG1’s proposal to pair holiday status with worker protections
objection: If the proposal only works when it is paired with enforceable paid time-to-vote protections, then the holiday itself is redundant; the real policy effect comes from the worker-protection rules, not the holiday designation.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is necessary to shift baseline schedules and household routines
objection: Even if schools or some workplaces close, low-income parents still depend on services and jobs that can continue on holidays, so the holiday does not reliably remove the practical voting barriers those families face.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday lowers transaction costs by making voting the default and reducing requests for time off
objection: Unless private employers are required to close or pay workers, hourly employees still have to navigate employer discretion, request time, and potentially deal with denied requests or lost wages. So the supposed reduction in transaction costs is not reliable for the people most constrained.

target: AG1’s argument that holiday status is complementary to time-to-vote laws
objection: If the main turnout mechanism is enforceable paid time-to-vote protection, then the holiday adds little and may even distract from the more direct and dependable reform of employer scheduling and pay rules.

A holiday does not meaningfully change what private-sector workers can actually do if their employers still keep them on duty or do not provide paid leave. In that case, the same uncertainty and pay tradeoff remain, so time-to-vote laws address the problem more directly.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday changes the labor-market environment enough to make employers more likely to grant paid time or reduce hours
objection: Holiday status only changes the calendar label; it does not ensure pay continuity or prevent employers from scheduling around the holiday. For many low-income workers, the practical result can still be lost wages or lost voting time, making the holiday an unreliable tool.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday also helps election administration and shortens waits
objection: Even if more people are off work, the transcript provides no reliable basis for assuming a holiday will improve election administration enough to matter; the more dependable way to reduce turnout barriers remains direct employer time-to-vote protections and registration reforms.
